People / tribal nation

Kiowa

Kiowa histories connect northern and southern Plains movement, Texas and Oklahoma, while the present Kiowa Tribe publishes accounts of its government and community institutions. This foundation brings a short Tribal history together with an edited treaty, dated education reporting, a Kiowa educator’s first-person reflection, a collaborative scholarly account and art history. Alliances, the wider people, present institutions and individual voices retain their own scope. Additional reading brings an earlier primary agreement, community remembrance and a partially inspected local land-history study into the foundation.

Source & image record ↗ · Public domain — SAAM item marked Free to use

Smithsonian American Art Museum identifies the sitter as Téh-tóot-sah, also known as Tohausen or Little Bluff, a Kiowa chief, and dates George Catlin’s oil portrait to 1834. Its actual subject classification explicitly names Kiowa. This is an outside artist’s historical portrait of an individually identified person, not a generic Native likeness, a documentary photograph, Kiowa-made art, or a current tribal-government representative. Exact portrait location, clothing/design meanings, current cultural practice and community endorsement are not established by this image check. A Kiowa people-and-Tribe starting route, with separate scopes for the government, named artists and an educator's experience. Plains Apache and Comanche alliances do not merge identities. Only annual-report pp. 24, 39–40 and 45 and the recorded selected text were inspected; image-only museum pages remain unread.

  1. History of the Kiowa Tribe — official historical account

    The Kiowa Tribe's own short history provides a first orientation to movement, alliances and reservation change, with disputed early chronology left open.

  2. Our Story — Kiowa early-childhood language learning and a proposed theory of learning

    Melody Windsong Redbird-Post's first-person education account connects family experience, immersion teaching and proposed work without treating plans as outcomes.

  3. Kiowa Six — art-historical essay

    This museum-authored essay introduces six named artists and their painting and mural work while its inconsistent dates and gender generalizations remain qualified.

  4. Kiowa Tribe Annual Report FY 2025–2026 — selected education, language and community-communication pages

    Selected annual-report pages show how the Tribe describes education, language and community communication in a defined fiscal period.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

A people, a present Tribe and related reading routes

Kiowa is a people-level reading route, while the Kiowa Tribe’s publications describe a present government and its institutions in Oklahoma. The Tribe’s history discusses alliances with Comanche and Plains Apache people. Those relationships do not make the names interchangeable: Plains Apache has its own directory route, and shared treaties or institutions do not by themselves establish one timeless identity.

Read the sources [1] Kiowa Tribe [3] Kiowa Tribe

02

Movement, Texas connections and uncertain early dates

The Tribe’s historical account and Kracht’s article both describe movement from the northern toward the southern Plains and connections with present-day Texas. Their Black Hills chronologies differ. These accounts provide a broad route into the history; precise origins, dates and archaeological identifications need further research. The Atlas does not turn a migration outline into a fixed homeland boundary or treat a community history page as an inspected archaeological report.

Read the sources [1] Kiowa Tribe [8] Oklahoma Historical Society, The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture

03

Horses, bison and historical livelihoods

The Tribe’s overview describes historical mobility, bison hunting, horse use and gathering. Read that account in its period and regional setting. It helps explain the Southern Plains history being discussed, while contemporary education, work and family life require their own sources rather than a picture of every Kiowa person living in one historical way.

Read the sources [1] Kiowa Tribe

04

Reading the 1867 Medicine Lodge treaty

The edited October 21, 1867 Kiowa and Comanche treaty includes reservation and conditional hunting provisions, promises of federal services, a requirement concerning later land cessions and compulsory schooling in English branches. Its terms give readers a primary document to examine. They do not alone prove implementation, universal consent or present-day rights. This named instrument should also be distinguished from the separate treaty involving Kiowa, Comanche and Apache representatives.

Read the sources [5] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties

05

Reservation change and the limits of this first history

The Tribal history and Kracht’s account describe reservation confinement, allotment and settlement pressures. Their compressed narratives are starting points for reviewing nineteenth-century Texas and Oklahoma history. The original military, removal, allotment and implementation records have not been read in this foundation, so precise legal conclusions, landownership totals and a complete chronology remain open.

Read the sources [1] Kiowa Tribe [8] Oklahoma Historical Society, The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture [5] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties

06

Education as a contemporary institution

The Tribe’s FY 2025–2026 report describes its Education Agency across child care, school partnerships, higher education, career learning and community activities. It presents Kiowa language, heritage and contemporary life as part of its educational aims. These are the institution’s reported purposes and activities. The Atlas does not promise assistance, repeat financial figures or treat the report as an independent evaluation of results.

Read the sources [3] Kiowa Tribe

07

Community news and editorial perspective

The Tribe’s FY2025–2026 report describes Media & Outreach as a communication service for Tribal members, programs and departments. It identifies the newsletter, website and event calendar among its channels and says community members may contribute announcements, editorials and other submissions. The report also describes editorial discretion and a final-content approval process. This helps readers understand how one community institution presents information; it does not establish independent reporting, participation outcomes or representation of every Kiowa perspective.

Read the sources [3] Kiowa Tribe

08

Language teaching across classrooms and families

The same dated report describes a teacher-credentialing process and language classes delivered in schools, community settings and online. Melody Windsong Redbird-Post’s first-person essay gives another perspective: she recounts child-care language work, family learning and collaboration with elders, educators and parents. Her experience and future project plans remain attributed to her; neither source supplies a verified current count of speakers or proof of every learner’s proficiency.

Read the sources [3] Kiowa Tribe [4] LearnKiowa [9] Kiowa Tribe, Kiowa Language Department

09

Community listening and a shared classroom

In their 2018 article, Rachel C. Jackson with Kiowa Elder Dorothy Whitehorse DeLaune describe the Kiowa Clemente course and a classroom shaped by community interests. Their account explains how listening, shared decisions and language work inform their teaching. This is a situated educational interpretation and relationship, not a rule for every Kiowa person or a present course schedule. Specific stories, songs and culturally governed materials in the publication are not retold here.

Read the sources [6] Community Literacy Journal; public copy hosted by University of Science and Arts of Oklahoma

10

Named artists and the Kiowa Six

Lydia L. Wyckoff’s art-historical essay identifies Jack Hokeah, Monroe Tsatoke, Spencer Asah, James Auchiah, Stephen Mopope and Lois Smoky within the group known as the Kiowa Six or Kiowa Five. It follows their painting, university-era work and mural commissions. The essay describes plain backgrounds and areas of flat color as part of this history. These are named artists and an art-group label; the account does not define all Kiowa art or authorize reuse of the artworks.

Read the sources [7] Encyclopedia of the Great Plains, University of Nebraska–Lincoln; author affiliation printed as Philbrook Museum of Art

11

An earlier agreement at the Little Arkansas

The 1865 agreement predates Medicine Lodge. Its reservation provisions sit alongside written-permission requirements for hunting travel and rules about where people could camp. Article 6 discusses people not present at the council. Reading those clauses together helps distinguish the written agreement from universal assent or actual implementation; they do not determine current land rights.

Read the sources [10] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database

12

Palo Duro in community memory

The District 7 newsletter describes the 2024 commemoration of the 1874 Battle of Palo Duro Canyon as a setting for remembrance and public education involving several Southern Plains communities. This is a dated community account of how history is remembered and shared. Its battle narrative still needs comparison with Kiowa testimony and original military and civilian records.

Read the sources [11] Kiowa Tribe, District 7 Legislative Office

13

Later land loss as a local historical question

Palmer’s 2011 study examines later Kiowa allotment sales through land-tenure applications and geographic comparison. He describes economic needs, relocation and divided inheritance as factors within his case-study area. He also notes difficulty separating relocation policy’s effects. This attributed local analysis is not a current ownership assessment or a single explanation for every Kiowa family’s history.

Read the sources [12] American Indian Culture and Research Journal / UCLA American Indian Studies Center; eScholarship repository

14

Reading path and unfinished coverage

Read community publications alongside the actual 1865 and 1867 agreements, keeping promises, interpretation and implementation separate. The newsletter offers a dated route into remembrance; Palmer’s partially accessible study extends the land-history questions. Nine substantive works form a reviewed foundation, with substantial gaps in Texas primary evidence, community-authored historical depth and later history. No completion or community endorsement is claimed.
